one_liner: Pure-Julia recursive multithreaded matmul that beat 6-thread OpenBLAS on small and medium matrices in a 2020 run.
what_it_does: Gaius provides dense matrix multiplication only: Gaius.mul!(C, A, B), Gaius.mul(A, B) and single-threaded mul_serial!/mul_serial for Float64, Float32, Int64, Int32 and Int16 matrices, views, adjoints and transposes, plus complex matrices stored as StructArrays (split real and imaginary arrays). These are separate, unexported functions with the same argument order as LinearAlgebra.mul!; there is no 5-argument alpha/beta form and no other BLAS routine. The author now presents it as an unmaintained teaching playground and points users to Octavian.jl and Tullio.jl.
how_it_is_fast: Recursive divide-and-conquer GEMM: C, A and B are split into 2x2 sub-blocks (k split in half), three quadrants are handed to Threads.@spawn tasks and the fourth runs on the caller, recursing until a block falls under a block size (64, or 96 with AVX-512F; 32 for small problems) or a per-task work budget of m*n*k/(8*nthreads). Leaf blocks run a plain triple loop vectorised by LoopVectorization.jl's @avx, and Julia's depth-first task scheduler lets calls nest inside other threaded code. Complex products run as four real GEMMs on the split arrays; there is no packing of A and B as in OpenBLAS's GotoBLAS-style kernels.
when_to_use: Square-ish Float64 or Float32 products in roughly the 10-650 range (Float32) or 10-800 range (Float64), where the README plots show it ahead of 6-thread OpenBLAS
Integer matrices (Int64, Int32, Int16): OpenBLAS has no integer GEMM and Julia's generic fallback is single-threaded, which is what the README's integer plots compare against
Matmuls issued from inside already-parallel Julia code, where Gaius's task-based threading composes with the caller instead of oversubscribing cores like a separately threaded BLAS
Complex products whose data already lives in StructArrays (split real and imaginary parts)
Reading or teaching a compact recursive GEMM (about 1,200 lines of Julia)
when_not_to_use: Large matrices: the README plots show OpenBLAS ahead beyond about 800 (Float64) and 650 (Float32); in chriselrod's April 2020 multithreaded run (issue #11, AVX-512 machine) Gaius blocked_mul! took 5.516 s at 9737x9737 against 0.891 s for OpenBLAS 0.3.9 and 0.889 s for MKL
Production code: the README says it is not stable or well tested and not actively maintained; Octavian.jl is the maintained, faster pure-Julia BLAS
Anything beyond C = A*B: no alpha/beta scaling, no gemv-style BLAS API, no trsm, syrk or LAPACK
Interleaved Matrix{ComplexF64} or other element types (Rational, Dual, Float16): Gaius.mul! only accepts the five real types and StructArray complex
Tiny matrices: the plots show OpenBLAS ahead around 2x2, and each threaded call allocates (80 allocations, about 10 KiB at 104x104 in the README)

integration.dependencies: LoopVectorization 0.12.10+, VectorizationBase 0.20-0.21, StructArrays 0.5-0.6, UnsafeArrays 1.0.1, plus the LinearAlgebra and Random stdlibs
integration.min_toolchain: Julia 1.5 per Project.toml (CI matrix: Julia 1.6, 1.8 and latest 1.x); the README benchmarks used Julia 1.4.0-rc2
integration.platforms: Any CPU LoopVectorization supports; CI runs Linux, Windows and macOS on x64 and 32-bit x86; block size 96 with AVX-512F, else 64
integration.thread_safety: README: spawns tasks on Julia's depth-first scheduler so calls can be nested inside multithreaded programs; the Adjoint StructArray complex methods temporarily negate A's imaginary array in place, so A must not be read concurrently during such a call
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — Gaius.mul!(C, A, B) mirrors the 3-argument LinearAlgebra.mul! call for supported element types, but it is a separate unexported function (call it qualified), has no alpha/beta form and covers matmul only

gotchas: The README's first REPL example now calls an unqualified mul! on both the 'from LinearAlgebra' and the 'from Gaius' line; commit 2892760 shows the original line was blocked_mul!, renamed in a January 2021 README edit. Gaius does not export mul!, so as written both lines call LinearAlgebra.mul!. The published timings and plots come from the 2020 blocked_mul! code on Julia 1.4.0-rc2, before the January 2021 threading API change (#57, #63) and tkf's November 2021 rebalancing (#83, #88). The current release needs Julia 1.5+, so the numbers cannot be reproduced on it as published.

Covector path: the CoVecTypes methods of _mul! and _mul_add! compute k = size(A, 1), which is 1 for an adjoint or transposed vector, so v'*A never enters the blocked or threaded branch and always runs one single-threaded kernel; the unreachable branch passes Val(factor) to block_covec_mat_mul!/block_covec_vec_mul!, which have no such method. Issue #79 'Covector-matrix multiplication is broken' (bug) has been open since March 2021.

Adjoint and transpose StructArray complex methods mutate inputs as an 'ugly hack' (source comment): A.parent.im is negated before the four real GEMMs and restored afterwards, and C.parent.im is negated at the end; an exception mid-call leaves A negated.

sizecheck=false skips all dimension checks (README: 'bad, segfaulty things can happen'); zero-size dimensions are not special-cased before the @avx kernels, and LoopVectorization's README lists iterating an empty loop as undefined behaviour.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No sibling in this category is a dense GEMM (TriangularSolve.jl does triangular solves on the same LoopVectorization stack, FFTA.jl does FFTs); for matmul, the catalog's Octavian.jl (wave 8) is the maintained and faster pure-Julia choice. Pick Gaius only for its simple recursive code, or for threaded integer matmul nested inside parallel Julia code.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run in 2020 on a 6-core Ryzen 5 2600 (Zen+, AVX2) with Julia 1.4.0-rc2 (LLVM 8) and 6 threads, against OpenBLAS (version unstated) set to 6 threads. 104x104 Float64 mul! took 31.2 us vs 68.5 us (about 2.2x, derived), 150x150 split-complex about 1.06x, and the log-log plots show OpenBLAS ahead at about 2x2 and beyond 800 (Float64) / 650 (Float32). All of this was measured with the pre-2021 blocked_mul! code, and no benchmark script is in the repo.
status_note: Abandoned: the last commit (2023-05-05, v0.6.8) only fixed loading under Static.StaticInt, and the README says it is not maintained or well tested; it is MIT, registered and small enough to read, but use Octavian.jl when speed matters.
